title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is looking for space curves (y(x), z(x)) that make ∫V dx stationary, where V depends on x, y, z and their derivatives p=y', p'=z' (and, more generally, higher derivatives q, r, ...). He writes dV = M dx + N dy + N' dz + P dp + P' dp' (+ Q dq + ...). On the previous pages he obtained the two Euler–Lagrange equations by a trick. He treats z(x) as a known function and solves a one-variable problem for y, then does the same with the roles exchanged. This gives N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − ... = 0 and N' − dP'/dx + d²Q'/dx² − ... = 0.

This page: (§9 end) The solution holds whatever order of derivatives appears in V. (§10) Because higher-order problems are usually intractable, he restricts to first-order Lagrangians V(x, y, z, p, p'). The system is then I. N dx = dP and II. N' dx = dP', i.e. ∂V/∂y = d/dx ∂V/∂y' and ∂V/∂z = d/dx ∂V/∂z'.

(§11) He adds a third, dependent equation that is useful in calculation. Multiply I by p and II by p' (using dy = p dx, dz = p' dx); this gives N dy = p dP and N' dz = p' dP'. Substitute into dV: dV = M dx + p dP + P dp + p' dP' + P' dp' = M dx + d(pP + p'P'). Setting S = V − Pp − P'p', this gives (on the next page) M dx = dS, i.e. d/dx (V − y'V_{y'} − z'V_{z'}) = ∂V/∂x. In modern terms: dH/dx = −∂L/∂x with H = Σ p_i ∂L/∂p_i − L. When V has no explicit x, H is constant: the Beltrami/energy first integral for two dependent variables.

The next page notes that any one of the three equations follows from the other two. It then applies the system to ∫ x y' z' dx, where the y- and z-equations integrate at once to qx = a, px = b.
errors: No error on this page; the derivation of M dx = d(V − Pp − P'p') is correct.

Minor gap (next page): the claim that any one of the three equations follows from the other two is only true generically. Recovering I (or II) from the third equation plus the other one requires p ≠ 0 (resp. p' ≠ 0). The third equation is implied by I and II unconditionally.

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equations for a functional with two dependent variables (space curves), obtained by freezing one unknown function and varying the other
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange system for several dependent variables
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–62 δ-method papers), with Euler's own treatment in the Methodus inveniendi (1744) and later papers
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (E65, 1744) for the related constrained and several-function cases; Euler's later variational papers in Novi Commentarii (E296 etc.); this paper E740

ideas.what: Third (dependent) equation M dx = d(V − pP − p'P') for first-order Lagrangians with two unknowns
ideas.modern_name: Energy/Hamiltonian identity dH/dx = −∂L/∂x; second Weierstrass–Erdmann (du Bois-Reymond) form; Beltrami identity; Noether conservation law for x-translation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (one-variable case, Methodus 1744: V − Pp = const when M = 0); Beltrami (1868) for the name; Erdmann (1877) for the corner condition; Noether (1918) for the general principle
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65), chapter II, for one dependent variable. The two-variable version appears here in E740 and in Lagrange's treatment of space curves.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine extension of Euler's own Methodus results (Euler–Lagrange equations and the first integral V − pP = const) to space curves with two dependent variables. Lagrange's 1760 work and standard histories already cover this. Nothing on the page appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially accurate. In §11 the '1°.' and '2°.' labels are correct, and the 'sive' line reads ∂V = M∂x + ∂.(pP + p'P').
Next-page transcription (not this page): 'dV = pq dx + px dp + px dq' should read 'pq dx + qx dp + px dq'. This is consistent with P = qx, P' = px stated there.
